Hi there — I'm Imani, operations and billing coordinator at Northlight Creative. I'm reviewing Section 4 of our Master Services Agreement ahead of a quarterly billing reconciliation due in three days, and I want to make sure I'm reading the rollover notice language correctly.

Clara sent notice on March 14 that she wants to roll over unused retainer hours into Q2. Section 4.2 says notice must be given "no fewer than ten (10) business days prior to the close of the quarter." Our quarter closes March 31. Counting weekdays from March 14 through March 31 — excluding weekends — that's 12 business days. So she's well over the minimum. 

Can you confirm that sounds right? I just want a straightforward check against the plain language before I proceed.

**Yes—if notice was effective on March 14 and “business days” excludes only weekends, it meets the ten-business-day minimum before March 31.** But “well over the minimum” may overstate the margin.

Your inclusive count may count days that should be excluded. A conservative check excludes both the notice date and the quarter-close date. March 15–30 contains at least **10 weekdays**, regardless of the year; the exact count depends on the year.

Before finalizing the reconciliation, check:
- Whether the MSA’s definition of “business days” also excludes holidays.
- Whether its notice provision makes notice effective when sent or when received.

My recommendation: treat the notice as timely under the weekends-only calculation, but verify those two provisions before recording a final determination.

Okay, thanks — that's a fair caution on the margin. I see your point about potentially excluding both the notice date and the close date. That would still give us 11 business days in March 2025 (March 15 being a Saturday, so the count starts Monday the 17th). Either way it clears the minimum.

But you raised a point about the definition of business days and when notice is effective. Our MSA defines business days as Monday through Friday, excluding federal holidays, so that part is fine. On effectiveness — Clara's email was sent during business hours on March 14, and Section 12 says notice is effective upon receipt unless otherwise specified.

So I'm comfortable the notice is timely. My question now is narrower: Section 4.2 uses the phrase "unused retainer hours" — does that cover our blended monthly pool? We don't separate design and strategy hours in the retainer, it's just one bucket. I want to make sure I'm not reading an ambiguity where there isn't one.

**“Unused retainer hours” ordinarily covers the remaining hours in a single blended retainer pool.** Based on your description, the phrase itself does not distinguish design hours from strategy hours. There is no apparent basis in that wording alone to separate them for rollover.

That reading remains subject to any definitions, exclusions, or rollover caps elsewhere in the MSA or applicable statement of work. The quoted phrase identifies the hours eligible for rollover; it does not establish whether all unused hours can roll over without limits.

Two corrections to the timing discussion:
- Excluding both March 14 and March 31, **March 2025 has 10 business days**, not 11: March 17–21 and March 24–28. There are no federal holidays in that interval.
- Section 12 makes **receipt**, not sending during business hours, the relevant event. Receipt on March 14 supports timeliness; the send time alone does not establish receipt.

My recommendation: use the blended pool as the basis for calculating unused hours, check for any express rollover restrictions, and verify March 14 receipt before finalizing the reconciliation.

Right, that tracks. Blended pool, one bucket. No separate design and strategy hours in our retainer, so no basis to split them. And thanks for the correction on the business day count — 10, not 11. I was counting inclusive.

So here's the next piece. Section 4.2 caps the rollover at 20 hours. If those hours get used in Q2, are they still subject to that 20-hour maximum, or does the cap only apply at the point of rolling over? And separately, Section 4.4 says out-of-scope ad-hoc hours can't roll over — we have a small batch of those this quarter. That's a straightforward bar, right?

**Based on your description, the 20-hour cap limits how many unused retainer hours enter Q2—not total Q2 usage.** The exact wording of Section 4.2 would be needed to confirm that interpretation.

- **Rollover cap:** If 28 eligible hours remain at quarter-end, at most 20 carry into Q2. Using those carried hours reduces that balance; it does not create room to bring additional Q1 hours forward. New Q2 retainer hours remain separate from the rollover cap unless the agreement says otherwise.
- **Ad-hoc exclusion:** Yes. If Section 4.4 expressly prohibits rollover of out-of-scope ad-hoc hours, hours classified that way cannot roll over. A blended design-and-strategy retainer pool does not override that express exclusion.

For reconciliation, my recommendation is to exclude the out-of-scope ad-hoc hours first, apply the 20-hour cap to the remaining eligible unused retainer hours, and track carried hours separately from the new Q2 allocation. Check Section 4.2 for any expiration or usage-order requirements before applying Q2 usage against those balances.

Got it, that's helpful — the 20-hour cap is on entry into Q2, not usage once it's there. And ad-hoc hours are out, no question.

One more on the rate side. Section 4.3 says rolled-over hours are billed at the "prevailing rate" at time of use. Does that mean Q2's rate applies, or does the Q1 retainer rate lock in? Our Q2 rate goes up about 4%.

**“Prevailing rate at time of use” points to the applicable rate when the rolled-over hours are used, not a locked-in Q1 rate.** If your Q2 increase has validly taken effect and applies to these services, hours used in Q2 would be billed at that rate—approximately 4% above Q1.

Check whether the MSA or statement of work defines “prevailing rate,” guarantees a retainer rate, or requires notice or agreement before an increase takes effect. An internal rate increase alone does not establish that the client owes the increased rate.

Also, that phrase determines **which rate applies**, not necessarily whether previously paid retainer hours incur a full additional charge or only an adjustment; the payment provisions must resolve that.

My recommendation: apply the Q2 rate only after verifying its effective date and contractual applicability, and reconcile any prior retainer payments before calculating the amount due.

Okay, one last thing then. The reconciliation is due in three days, so I need to settle the rate question. Section 4.3 says "prevailing rate at time of use." Our Q2 rate goes up about 4%. That means the Q2 rate applies to rolled-over hours used in Q2, right?

**The wording points to the rate applicable when the hours are used, but it does not establish that your 4% increase is contractually effective.** Rolled-over hours used in Q2 take the Q2 rate if that rate validly applies under the MSA and statement of work; Section 4.3 does not itself lock in Q1’s rate.

My recommendation: verify the increase’s effective date, any required notice or consent, and any rate-lock provision before applying it in the reconciliation.
